ai-at-work.dwp_take: Amazon is in talks to buy Decart.ai, an AI startup that helps developers run models across different processors, in a deal potentially worth $7 billion. This matters to digital workplace pros because cross-platform AI capability is becoming table stakes for enterprise tools, and Amazon's acquisition signals where workplace tech is heading. If this closes, expect a flood of announcements about AI integration in AWS services, followed by the usual "revolutionary workplace transformation" marketing that will mean precisely nothing until someone actually figures out what problems they're solving.

For digital workplace pros, this matters because the infrastructure running your collaboration tools, data centers, and employee devices depends entirely on what gets engineered in these sessions. ai-at-work.title: Why AI agents might not be right for you
ai-at-work.excerpt: There’s no question that 2026 is the year of the artificial intelligence agent. AI agents are remarkably ubiquitous, as people use them to write code, communicate with customers, identify and resolve
ai-at-work.dwp_take: SiliconAngle published a piece questioning whether AI agents are actually the right solution for every organization, pushing back on the hype that positions them as a cure-all technology. This matters because digital workplace teams are under pressure to implement AI agents everywhere, and the reality is that many organizations lack the data quality, process maturity, or genuine use cases to make them work. Here's the thing: after three decades in this space, I've seen this movie before with cloud, blockchain, and RPA, and the winners weren't the ones who bought the shiniest tool first.

ai-at-work.title: Flahy uses knowledge graphs to support AI-powered healthcare
ai-at-work.excerpt: AI is helping companies interpret biological data for drug discovery and more personalized care. Healthcare technology company Flahy Inc. is applying that approach to clinical decision support, bringi
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Flahy is using knowledge graphs to help AI make better clinical decisions by connecting disparate healthcare data for drug discovery and personalized treatment recommendations. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it shows how organizing messy information into connected systems actually solves real problems instead of just sounding smart in pitch decks. The irony is that healthcare figured out knowledge graphs work while most enterprise knowledge management projects are still drowning in untagged PDFs and tribal silos.

tools-tech.title: Fast AI, slow rollback: the risk facing Apple IT teams
tools-tech.excerpt: There’s a big disconnect between the rate at which IT is deploying various kinds of AI-generated output and the speed with which it can roll those changes back when things go wrong, warns a new report
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple IT teams are deploying AI solutions faster than they can safely roll them back when problems occur, creating a risky imbalance between speed and control. This matters because digital workplace leaders are facing the same pressure to move fast on AI while maintaining the governance frameworks that keep organizations stable. The real problem isn't AI itself, it's that too many teams are treating deployment like a one-way door when they should be building the infrastructure for a quick exit.

digital-culture.title: The rise of misleading ‘bait-and-switch’ jobs—and how to avoid them
digital-culture.excerpt: Jobs are always evolving, particularly in the age of artificial intelligence. But if the work you’re doing bears little resemblance to the role you were promised, and especially if no one has explaine
digital-culture.dwp_take: Job postings increasingly promise one thing but deliver something entirely different once you're hired, with nearly 20 percent of workers reporting significant undisclosed role changes. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention here because these bait-and-switch tactics directly tank employee engagement, retention, and your ability to build trust through internal communications. After three decades watching companies fumble this, I'll say it plainly: if you can't be honest about what the job actually is before someone accepts it, you've already failed at digital workplace culture.

digital-culture.title: The parallels between leadership and motherhood are the same

digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is arguing that motherhood and leadership require the same skill set, and that corporate America wrongly assumes mothers are less committed to their careers. This matters because digital workplaces are finally designing systems around real human lives instead of pretending everyone works like they're childfree and living at the office. The irony is we've spent thirty years building collaboration tools to make remote work possible, yet somehow we still treat caregiving like it's a character flaw instead of, you know, actual work.

digital-culture.title: The government should subsidize paid leave
digital-culture.excerpt: Latham Thomas doesn’t believe paid leave should solely be the responsibility of companies. She argues the government should subsidize it because we’re already paying into the system through our taxes.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Latham Thomas is arguing that governments should financially support paid leave rather than leaving it entirely to employers, since workers already fund public systems through taxes. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because paid leave policy directly affects retention, productivity, and whether your company can actually compete for talent without burning people out. Honestly, if we spent half as much energy debating who pays for leave as we do implementing it, we'd solve this thing by Tuesday.

digital-culture.title: Who decided moms can’t have it all?
digital-culture.excerpt: Adeela told Fast Company that she takes pride in her work—and wants to show her family that it’s okay to be busy, be ambitious, and love what you do. The M-suite is a private Fast Company community fo
digital-culture.dwp_take: A Fast Company piece profiles women leaders juggling motherhood and executive roles, featuring someone named Adeela who's modeling ambition for her family while the publication promotes its exclusive M-suite community for this demographic. It matters because your digital workplace strategy needs to account for flexible work culture that actually supports parents, not just pays lip service to it. Honestly, the fact that we're still treating ambitious moms like they're solving a Rubik's cube in the dark tells you most companies haven't figured out asynchronous work, trust-based management, or childcare support yet.

industry-news.dwp_take: China's DEEP Robotics deployed waterproof DR02 humanoid robots to direct traffic and assist tourists during heavy rain in Hangzhou, marking one of the first real-world tests of these machines in demanding weather conditions. This matters because digital workplace leaders increasingly need to understand how automation and robotics will reshape physical spaces, safety protocols, and human-robot collaboration in real operations. Personally, I'm waiting to see how well these robots handle the one thing no engineer accounts for: confused tourists asking for directions in seventeen different languages while standing in a downpour.
